question.text: What is the theoretical relationship between USDINR call option premium and USDINR put option premium with the same strike and expiry?

answer.text: Put-call parity for currency options: C - P = S × e^(-rf×T) - K × e^(-rd×T), where rf is USD rate and rd is INR rate
C = P always for the same strike and expiry
C - P = S - K at all times
There is no relationship between USDINR call and put premiums

explanation.text: The Logic: European-style options on the same underlying with the same strike and expiry are linked by put-call parity. For a currency option pair on, say, USDINR, the parity relationship can be written with both rates discounted explicitly: C - P = S × e^(-rf×T) - K × e^(-rd×T), where rf is the foreign-currency interest rate (USD) and rd is the domestic-currency interest rate (INR). Both the spot and the strike are discounted because each currency in the pair earns interest. The Trap: Call and put premiums are not always equal (they coincide only around the at-the-money forward). The simple equity-style C - P = S - K ignores discounting. And there is a definite mathematical relationship between the two — it is not "no relationship". Note: The NISM Series I (Currency Derivatives) workbook pages reviewed cover generic European put-call parity (C + PV(X) = P + S) and interest-rate parity for currency futures, but the explicit currency-option parity equation with separate domestic and foreign discount factors was not located in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general FX-option-theory industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
